issues.legal_issue: Self-acquired immovable property can become part of a customary impartible estate when its holder intends to incorporate it.
material_facts: The estate was ancestral, belonged to an undivided Hindu family, and descended by primogeniture.
The dispute concerned whether immovable properties acquired after the original grant had become part of the impartible estate.
The Court found that incorporation depends on the intention of the holder, which may be inferred from conduct and other evidence.
issues.conclusion: A holder of a customary impartible estate may incorporate self-acquired immovable property into it by declaring that intention; the property then acquires the estate’s incidents, including impartibility and descent by primogeniture, unless statute or custom excludes that power.
issues.legal_principle: Under Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Devi, a customary impartible ancestral estate remains joint family property insofar as the right of survivorship survives, even though partition and certain other ordinary joint-family rights do not. The power to incorporate self-acquired immovable property depends on the holder’s intention and may be excluded by statute or custom. The Court also referred to Collector of Madura v. Mootoo Ramalinga Sathupathy on the recognition of proven usage.

predicates.partition_suit: The dispute arises in a suit seeking partition of property claimed to belong to a joint family.
predicates.customary_impartible_estate: The family holds an estate that custom makes indivisible and that descends to a single heir.
predicates.self_acquired_immovable_property: The holder acquired the immovable property separately rather than receiving it as part of the estate.
predicates.holder_intended_incorporation: The holder’s declaration, conduct, or other evidence shows an intention to make the acquired property part of the impartible estate.
predicates.incorporation_power_excluded: A statute or family custom prevents the holder from incorporating the property.

issues.definition: When a partition dispute concerns separately acquired immovable property and the holder of a customary impartible estate intended to incorporate it, the property becomes impartible unless that power was excluded.

issues.legal_issue: A family custom, rather than incorporation, may make a category of movable property impartible if the custom is adequately proved.
material_facts: The partition dispute concerned jewels claimed to be ceremonial regalia of the estate.

Evidence included a family member’s will describing state jewels as regalia and impartible, a list of jewels used at an installation ceremony, and family members’ statements and conduct treating ceremonial jewels as belonging to the estate.
The Court found the evidence sufficient to establish a family custom concerning some ceremonial jewels and upheld the finding that 38 jewels were regalia.
issues.conclusion: The doctrine of incorporation does not apply to movable property, but a proved family custom may make a category of movables impartible; the finding that 38 jewels were impartible regalia was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that incorporation applies to immovable, not movable, property. A family custom modifying ordinary law must be ancient and invariable and established by clear and unambiguous evidence. In assessing a family custom, the consensus, traditional beliefs, statements, and conduct of family members are relevant; fewer instances may suffice than for a territorial or community custom. The Court relied on Ramalakhmi Ammal v. Sivanantha Perumal Sethurayar and Abdul Hussein Khan v. Bibi Sona.

predicates.partition_suit: The dispute arises in a suit seeking partition of property claimed to belong to a joint family.
predicates.movable_property_claimed_as_family_regal: A party claims that movable property belongs to a ceremonial or regalia category that is not available for partition.
predicates.family_members_consistently_treated_the_: Family members’ beliefs, statements, or conduct show that they treated the relevant category of movables as belonging to the estate rather than as divisible family property.
predicates.clear_evidence_establishes_an_ancient_in: Clear and unambiguous evidence establishes a family practice as ancient and invariable.

issues.definition: When family members consistently treat a category of movables as impartible and clear evidence establishes an ancient and invariable family custom, that category is impartible in a partition suit.

issues.legal_issue: Immovable property incorporated into an estate listed as impartible is included in the statutory estate and is subject to the statutory restriction on alienation.
material_facts: The estate was included in the schedule to the legislation identifying impartible estates.
The disputed immovable properties had been acquired after the original grant but were claimed to have been incorporated into the estate before the legislation applied.
The Court held that property incorporated into the estate formed an integral part of it.
issues.conclusion: The scheduled estate includes immovable property incorporated into it before the legislation applied, and the statutory restrictions on alienation extend to that incorporated property.
issues.legal_principle: The Madras Impartible Estates Acts, including Madras Act II of 1904, defined and identified impartible estates and restricted alienation. The Court construed section 3 and the Schedule to include all impartible property constituting the listed estate, including property incorporated into it before the Act, and applied the statutory restriction on alienation to that property.

predicates.customary_impartible_estate_listed_as_im: The estate is an impartible estate identified in a statutory schedule.
predicates.immovable_property_incorporated_before_s: The holder incorporated the immovable property into the estate before the statutory regime applied to it.

issues.definition: If immovable property was incorporated into an estate identified as impartible before the statutory regime applied, the statutory restrictions governing that estate also govern the property.

issues.legal_issue: The residual building-vesting provision vests a building in the landholder who owned it immediately before vesting, not in other family members claiming ownership through survivorship.
material_facts: After the estate was taken over, a dispute arose in a partition suit about buildings that were not covered by the provision for specified administrative, institutional, or charitable buildings.
The holder of the estate owned the buildings immediately before the vesting date.
Other family members argued that their survivorship rights in the joint family estate made them persons who owned the buildings for purposes of the residual provision.
issues.conclusion: The residual building-vesting provision refers to the landholder and does not give other family members a right to claim the buildings under that provision.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 18(4) of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, a building outside the preceding categories vests in the person who owned it immediately before the notified date. Read with the Act’s definitions of landholder and principal landholder in section 2(8) and section 2(12), that expression refers to the landholder, not other members of the family. The Court also relied on the structure of sections 43 and 45, which provide for apportionment of compensation among a narrower class, to reject a construction giving a wider class rights under section 18(4).

predicates.estate_abolition_partition_dispute: The dispute concerns the effect of an estate-abolition law on property claimed in a partition proceeding.
predicates.building_falls_within_residual_building_: The building is not within a category of buildings dealt with by the special vesting provisions for administrative, institutional, or charitable uses.
predicates.landholder_owned_building_immediately_be: The landholder owned the building immediately before the vesting date.
predicates.family_members_claim_building_through_su: Other family members claim that their survivorship rights make them owners of the building for purposes of the vesting rule.

issues.definition: When a landholder owned a building in the residual category immediately before vesting, a family member’s survivorship claim does not make that member a person entitled to the building under the residual vesting rule.

issues.legal_issue: Property is incorporated into an impartible estate only when the evidence shows the holder intended to make it part of the estate.
material_facts: The Prince of Wales Market was built on land belonging to the estate to provide a public amenity in the estate’s principal town, and both lower courts found it had been incorporated.

The leasehold rights in nine villages arose from a settlement involving the estate; the estate holder actively participated, the lessee was treated as a nominee, and the rights were administered and treated as part of the estate.
The Court upheld the findings that the market and village leasehold rights were incorporated.
issues.conclusion: The Prince of Wales Market and the permanent leasehold rights in the nine villages were incorporated into the impartible estate.
issues.legal_principle: The decisive test for incorporation of immovable property is the holder’s intention, assessed from the evidence as a whole. Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Devi recognises the power to incorporate self-acquired immovable property into a customary impartible estate. Where both lower courts have found incorporation on the evidence, the Supreme Court found no reason to disturb the concurrent finding concerning the market.

predicates.partition_suit: The dispute arises in a suit seeking partition of property claimed to belong to a joint family.
predicates.customary_impartible_estate: The family holds an estate that custom makes indivisible and that descends to a single heir.
predicates.property_built_on_estate_land_for_public: The holder built the property on estate land to provide a public amenity in the estate’s principal town.
predicates.acquired_rights_administered_and_treated: The holder actively participated in acquiring the rights, and the rights were subsequently administered and treated as part of the estate.

issues.definition: In a partition suit concerning a customary impartible estate, property is incorporated when the evidence shows it was built on estate land for a public amenity or that acquired rights were administered and treated as part of the estate.

issues.legal_issue: The purchase and use of separate residences, without sufficiently clear evidence of an intention to incorporate them, does not make them part of an impartible estate.
material_facts: Five family residences outside the estate had been purchased separately.

The residences were in places convenient to the holder, and the family used them, but there was no reliable evidence that estate business was transacted there or that the holder intended to incorporate them.
The claimant relied on a trust deed, but the deed gave the beneficiary the same interest he would have received by inheritance and did not incorporate the residences into the impartible estate.
The Court upheld the finding that the residences had not been incorporated.
issues.conclusion: The five residences were not proved to have been incorporated into the impartible estate and remained partible.
issues.legal_principle: Incorporation depends on the holder’s intention, and the party asserting incorporation must establish it by evidence. The trust deed did not show an intention to confer a greater interest than the beneficiary would have received by inheritance; property not previously incorporated would therefore retain its partible character. The Court applied the incorporation principles stated in Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Devi.
